title: A Composite Index for Equality + Range
description: A query filtering one store over a date range has no supporting index; a composite (equality, range) index seeks the store then walks the dates. Why it matters: "one filter, one date range" is close to the most common query shape in business reporting -- getting the composite key order right is a core professional skill.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson combines two ideas that show up individually elsewhere in this course — composite indexes, and the equality-before-range column-ordering rule — into a single, extremely common real-world query shape: filtering by one specific thing (a store, a customer, a category) *and* a date range at the same time, with no existing index to support either part.

The scenario: a sales report wants one store's transactions for a single month — `WHERE StoreId = 7 AND SaleDate >= '2025-06-01' AND SaleDate < '2025-07-01'`. There's no supporting index at all, so even though the report only returns roughly 170 rows, answering it requires scanning the entire 400,000-row table, checking every row against both conditions one at a time.

This is a great lesson for reinforcing, in a single concrete example, the full equality-before-range design principle covered elsewhere in this course, because the query genuinely has one of each kind of condition: `StoreId = 7` is an **equality** condition — a single, exact, specific value — and `SaleDate >= ... AND SaleDate < ...` is a **range** condition — a continuous span of many possible values, not one exact value. The right composite index for this query is built with the equality column leading, and the range column following: `(StoreId, SaleDate)`.

Here's the intuition for exactly why that column order works so well, tying together how a B-tree index (the balanced, sorted tree structure SQL Server uses for indexes) actually gets used here. Picture the index as a phone book sorted first by store, and *within* each store's section, sorted by date. SQL Server can seek — jump almost directly, in a small, predictable number of steps — straight to the section belonging to store 7, using the equality condition. That narrows things down enormously in one single jump: instead of 400,000 rows, you're now looking at just this one store's chunk of the index, probably a few thousand rows out of the whole table. From there, because that chunk is *already* sorted by `SaleDate` internally, applying the range condition is cheap and direct: start reading right at June 1st, and simply keep reading forward until you pass July 1st, then stop. No searching, no checking irrelevant rows — just "start here, read forward until you're past the end of the range." Total work: one quick jump to the right store, then a short, contiguous read through exactly one month's worth of that store's data — landing at roughly the 170 rows the report actually needed, instead of touching all 400,000.

It's worth explicitly contrasting this with what would happen if the column order were flipped — `(SaleDate, StoreId)` instead. Then the index would be sorted first by date across *all* stores, and only *within* each date, sorted by store. The range condition (June's date range) could still be used to narrow things down to "just June's rows across every store," but within that range, store 7's rows would be scattered throughout each individual day's section rather than grouped together — so SQL Server would have to scan through the entirety of June's data (every store, every day in the range) and pick out only the store-7 rows along the way, doing significantly more work than the "store first, date second" version. This is exactly the composite-key-order lesson playing out again, and seeing it in a fresh, slightly different scenario (store + date, rather than customer + date) is genuinely useful for cementing the underlying principle as something you recognize on sight, rather than something tied to one specific example.

Why does this matter practically? "One specific entity, over a specific time window" is about as common a reporting pattern as exists in business software — one store's sales this month, one customer's activity this week, one warehouse's shipments today — and it's an extremely natural, intuitive thing for a developer or analyst to write without first checking whether a supporting index exists. Recognizing "this query has exactly one equality condition and one range condition" as an immediate cue for "I probably want a composite index with the equality column first" is one of the most broadly reusable diagnostic instincts you can build from this course.

A useful way to build lasting intuition here is to practice identifying the equality and range parts of a WHERE clause before you even think about indexes at all — just read the conditions and label each one. "`StoreId = 7`" — equality. "`SaleDate >= X AND SaleDate < Y`" — range. Once you've labeled them, the composite index design almost writes itself: equality columns lead, range columns follow. This labeling exercise works for far more complex queries too — a WHERE clause might have two or three equality conditions and one range condition, in which case all of the equality columns come first (in any order relative to each other, generally), with the range column trailing last, since it's the only one that can't be "seeked into" and must instead be scanned through once the equality conditions have already narrowed things down. Practicing this labeling on real queries from your own codebase is one of the fastest ways to turn this lesson's principle into an instinct you no longer have to consciously think through.

One more thing worth knowing: this exact index also tends to serve a whole family of related queries well, not just the one that motivated building it -- 'this store's sales in July,' 'this store's sales in the last 7 days,' 'this store's sales year to date' would all benefit from the same (StoreId, SaleDate) index, since they share the identical equality-then-range shape, just with a different specific date range plugged in each time.

As a final practical note, if you find yourself building several near-identical composite indexes just to handle slightly different combinations of equality columns, it's worth stepping back and considering whether a single, slightly wider composite index (equality columns first, in a sensible fixed order, range column last) could serve most of those query variations at once, rather than maintaining many narrow, single-purpose indexes.

## Scenario
A sales report pulls one store's transactions for a single month: `WHERE StoreId = 7 AND SaleDate >= '2025-06-01' AND SaleDate < '2025-07-01'`. There's no supporting index, so returning ~170 rows scans all 400,000.

## Why it's slow
The query combines an **equality** (`StoreId = 7`) with a **range** (`SaleDate` in June). With no index covering both, it's a **Clustered Index Scan**. The order of columns in the fix matters: you want to seek directly to store 7, then walk just its June rows.

## What to look for
- A full scan for a query that targets one store and one month.
- Reads proportional to the whole table, not to the small slice returned.

## The concept
Build a composite index with the **equality column first, the range column second**: `(StoreId, SaleDate)`. SQL Server seeks to `StoreId = 7`, and because the second key orders those rows by date, it then does a contiguous **range seek** over June. Put the range column first and you'd lose the ability to seek the store. INCLUDE `Amount` so the index also covers the SELECT.
startingQuery:
SELECT SaleId, SaleDate, Amount
FROM Sales
WHERE StoreId = 7
  AND SaleDate >= '2025-06-01' AND SaleDate < '2025-07-01';
hints: No index supports StoreId + SaleDate together, so the query scans the whole table.
You want to seek to the store first, then scan just its date range — so the equality column leads and the range column follows.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Sales_Store_Date ON Sales(StoreId, SaleDate) INCLUDE (Amount);
